title: India's Growing Network of Human Milk Banks Is Saving Premature Newborns
excerpt: A system of donor milk banks provides pasteurized breast milk to critically ill infants whose mothers cannot breastfeed, reducing mortality and serious complications in neonatal care units across the country.
body:
• India's human milk banking movement began in 1989 at Mumbai's Sion Hospital and has expanded to facilities across the country, though demand still outstrips supply.
  • Donor human milk significantly reduces the incidence of necrotizing enterocolitis (NEC), a severe intestinal condition that can be fatal in premature infants.
  • All donors undergo rigorous screening for communicable diseases and medications; milk is pasteurized at 62.5°C for 30 minutes before release.
  • The entire system operates on voluntary donations with no monetary transactions — donors are never paid and recipient families are never charged.

When a Mother Cannot Feed

The first instinct of most new mothers is to hold their baby close and breastfeed. But for some newborns — those born weeks too early, those separated from critically ill mothers, or those who have lost their mothers entirely — that first feed may never come naturally.

Human milk banks in India are built around a simple premise: a lactating mother donates surplus milk her own baby does not need, and through a regulated medical system, that milk reaches a newborn who cannot receive it from its own mother.

"Milk bank helps one mother save the baby of another mother," said Dr Poonam Sidana, director of neonatology and paediatrics at CK Birla Hospital, Delhi.

The movement traces back to 1989, when Dr Armida Fernandes established India's first human milk bank — and the first in Asia — at Sion Hospital in Mumbai. Since then, the network has expanded significantly, though Dr Satish Tiwari, founder of the Human Milk Banking Association of India, says the country still has a long way to go.

Why Donor Milk Matters for Fragile Infants

For premature and low-birth-weight babies, the issue goes beyond simple nutrition. Their digestive and immune systems are still developing, making them especially vulnerable to infections and severe complications.

The strongest medical evidence for donor milk centers on its ability to reduce necrotizing enterocolitis, or NEC — a condition that damages the intestine and can lead to life-threatening infection.

"Donor human milk is believed to bring down the incidence of necrotising enterocolitis and some infections more than formula does in premature babies."

— Dr Poonam Sidana, CK Birla Hospital, Delhi

Human milk contains bioactive and immune components that formula simply cannot replicate. But doctors are clear about the hierarchy: a mother's own milk, preferably through direct breastfeeding, remains the ideal. Donor milk is the next-best alternative when that first option is temporarily or permanently unavailable.

Dr Sakshi Goel, senior consultant at Madhukar Rainbow Children's Hospital, Delhi, described donor milk as a "transitional or supplemental resource" — critical for at-risk newborns, but not a replacement for establishing a mother's own lactation.

How the Donation System Works

A mother who wants to donate approaches a recognized milk bank or Comprehensive Lactation Management Centre, where she is counseled, screened medically, and assessed for eligibility. Only when her own baby's needs are fully met does the conversation turn to donation.

Donors are screened for communicable diseases including hepatitis B and C. Their medications are reviewed — psychotropic drugs, anti-cancer medications, and habit-forming substances all disqualify a donor. Smoking and alcohol consumption are also evaluated.

The donated milk then undergoes Holder pasteurization, heated to 62.5°C for 30 minutes and rapidly cooled. Samples are tested for bacterial contamination, and pasteurized milk is released only when cultures come back clean.

"Pasteurization processes modify various parts of human milk, especially a number of heat-sensitive enzymes and immune factors," Sidana said. "But it preserves the nutritional composition and many of the biological qualities while significantly improving safety."

Some centres have started using mobile collection vans that travel between hospitals and homes to expand the donor pool.

No Money Changes Hands

The entire system operates without financial transactions.

"Neither we give money or monetary benefit to the donor nor to the recipient. It is totally voluntary."

— Dr Satish Tiwari, Human Milk Banking Association of India

Tiwari strongly challenges the common belief that most mothers cannot produce enough milk, calling it "basically a misconception." In most cases, breastfeeding difficulties stem from delayed initiation, poor positioning, or the early introduction of formula — problems that lactation centres work to correct before considering donation.

Doctors also warn against informal milk sharing through friends or social media groups, where the safety safeguards of screening, pasteurization, and traceability disappear entirely. For fragile premature babies with already-compromised immune systems, the risks of unregulated milk can be serious.

The Gap Between Need and Supply

Despite progress, many milk banks remain unable to meet the full requirements of the hospitals they serve. Availability varies sharply between regions, and when demand exceeds local supply, the most vulnerable babies are prioritized.

At JIPMER's Amudham Thaipaal Maiyam, average voluntary milk collection has grown from roughly 400 millilitres per day in its early years to about 1,000 millilitres daily, with at least 20 premature infants benefiting each day.

Tiwari and his association continue to push for wider awareness through medical conferences, talks, and partnerships with organizations such as Rotary, which have helped fund equipment and infrastructure.

The message to mothers with surplus milk is straightforward: "Most of the mothers, they have more milk as compared to the requirement of her child," Tiwari said. "Mother or the relatives or the grandparent, they should not hesitate in donating the milk."
nri_angle: India's human milk banking system, started in Mumbai and now expanding nationwide, represents a healthcare innovation relevant to NRI families and medical professionals tracking Indian health advances.
